GROK
Updated 2026-09-14
Sources: your Grok bookmark folder (1248 posts)

NEW TODAY
- Folder now 1248 posts (11 new since Sep 13)
- Official (elonmusk Sep 14): Roadmap — Grok 4.7 roughly on par with Opus 5.0 (not 5.1); better in some ways, worse in others; need to fix multimodal. Grok 4.8 a noticeable improvement. Grok 4.9 probably Astra/Fable class. Grok 5 maybe better than anything
- Testers (cb_doge Sep 14): BREAKING summary of Elon’s roadmap (4.7≈Opus 5.0 → 4.8 → 4.9 Astra/Fable → 5 maybe best)
- Testers (cb_doge, XFreeze Sep 14): Grok 4.8 — 2.5T trained on SpaceXAI’s new C++ software stack; pretraining finishes this week, then RL; 4.7 still in final refinements
- Testers (testerlabor Sep 13): Colossus 2 still trains Imagine Video 2.0, Grok 4.7 Beta, Grok 5+
- Testers (nima_owji Sep 14): frames Elon as saying Grok 5 will be “AGI!” (tester headline; Elon’s text was “maybe better than anything”)
- Testers (DrstaOne Sep 13): rumor 4.7 this week / 2.1T / SpaceX+Starlink data (anticipation)
- Testers (Mr_Salio, MehdiCade Sep 13): satirical “Dario slowdown / ban open-source” delay framing — joke/satire, not a real agreement
- Testers (TheCaptainEli Sep 12): Copilot follow-on — Grok inside Microsoft Copilot as products-opening-doors framing

WHAT IT IS
- Grok is xAI / SpaceXAI's assistant: chat, voice, Imagine, Build, and the model API, in the Grok app, https://t.co/UvO8aC6o4n, and on X.
- This folder is Grok-the-product (app, models, voice, Imagine-in-Grok, plans). Separate folders exist for Grok Bot, Grok Build, and Grok Imagine.
- Grok Bot (persistent agents on a shared computer) and Grok Build (coding harness / Build mode) show up here when they ship inside SuperGrok or the Grok app.

GROK 4.6 / MODELS
- Official (elonmusk Sep 14): Roadmap — Grok 4.7 roughly on par with Opus 5.0 (not 5.1); better in some ways, worse in others; need to fix multimodal. Grok 4.8 a noticeable improvement. Grok 4.9 probably Astra/Fable class. Grok 5 maybe better than anything.
- Testers (cb_doge, XFreeze Sep 14): Grok 4.8 — 2.5T on SpaceXAI’s new C++ software stack; pretraining finishes this week then RL; 4.7 still in final refinements.
- Testers (testerlabor Sep 13): Colossus 2 still trains Imagine Video 2.0, Grok 4.7 Beta, Grok 5+.
- Testers (nima_owji Sep 14): frames Elon as saying Grok 5 will be “AGI!” (tester headline; Elon’s text was “maybe better than anything”).
- Testers (Mr_Salio, MehdiCade Sep 13): satirical “Dario slowdown / ban open-source” delay framing — joke/satire, not a real agreement.
- Official (elonmusk, grok, Microsoft365 Sep 12): Grok models in Microsoft Copilot — Word, Excel, PowerPoint (Frontier program first).
- Testers (XFreeze, joehansen Sep 12): Copilot = Grok on the office desk; Satya door-open + Elon confirm; still has to win the click.
- Testers (nima_owji, testerlabor Sep 12): 4.7 still cooking — RL length / early-quit / weak self-check; wait until 100% ready.
- Official (elonmusk Sep 11): Grok 4.7 needs a few more days — gives up too early on hard tasks / not rigorous enough self-check; possible over-penalized response length in RL.
- Testers (minchoi, LaceyPresley, testerlabor Sep 11): delay = refinement; stay on hard problems longer; don’t treat brevity as completion.
- Testers (Mr_Salio Sep 11): Sep 12 framed as end of Elon 10-day window + "grok-4-7-0907" (anticipation; then delayed).
- Testers (XFreeze Sep 11–12): intelligence-layer-across-workflow framing; SpaceXAI model-card anti-nerf jab; 4.7 soon.
- Testers (Dr_Singularity Sep 11): Millennium Prize / Grok 5 super-scientist trajectory (opinion).
- Testers (testerlabor, MehdiCade, Priyannkaaaa, XFreeze Sep 9–10): Grok 4.7 countdown ~2 days / Sat Sep 12; "grok-4-7-0907" still cited; 2.1T; Astra ~10x cheaper framing; OpenAI Pro-pause joke pull (anticipation / leak).
- Testers (Mr_Salio, Techkelvinx Sep 8): Grok 4.7 leak — release-style build id "grok-4-7-0907" reportedly staged (dated IDs previously marked Grok 4 ship days); still ~Sep 12; early talk cheaper than Astra / stronger agents / more SpaceX data (anticipation / leak).
- Testers (StatsWire Sep 7): 4.7 ~Sep 12; 2.1T; SpaceX engineering + Starlink supplemental; better token efficiency, slightly slower to serve.
- Testers (XFreeze Sep 8): Grok 4.6 #2 on updated AutomationBench-AA (agentic SaaS workflows) vs Fable 5.1 / GPT-5.6 / Kimi K3.
- Testers (joehansen Sep 7): Grok 4.6 high #2 on τ³-Banking at 50.7% (Qwen3.8 Max 51.3%; Muse Spark 1.3 max 50.5%).
- Testers (nextbigfuture Sep 8): frames GPT-6 as AGI and Grok 4.7 / Fable 5.2 as AGI or near-AGI from Dec 2026 onward (opinion).
- Grok 4.6 launched 2026-08-12. Elon: smart, fast, amazing bang for buck. Also #1 on Databricks.
- Same 1.5T base as 4.5; testers credit a big SFT + RL jump. Stronger multi-step reasoning, coding, agents, frontend taste.
- API: $2 input / $6 output per million tokens. Live in the Grok app, API, Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes Agent. Testers: also on Perplexity and Perplexity Computer.
- Reported leads: GDPVal-AA v2, AA-Briefcase, Harvey LAB; #1 CursorBench 3.2 (Extra High 70.8% at ~$2.81/task vs Fable 5 Max 70.5% at ~$17.32); #1 VISTA; #1 MedAgentBench; testers (joehansen, XFreeze): GPQA Diamond — 4.6 high led ~95%, then #2 at 94.9% after Gemini 3.8 Flash high took #1 at 95.3% (Sep 2). Testers: 4.6 High tied Opus 5 Max at 59 on the AA Agentic Index. Artificial Analysis ~61 — testers (XFreeze, cb_doge, Sep 4): ties newly released GPT-6 Astra at 61; beats Astra Max on Agentic Index 59 vs 51, τ³-Banking 51% vs 41%, non-hallucination 66% vs 49%, GDPval-AA v2 1,730 vs 1,629. Still matches GPT-5.6 Sol at up to 5x lower API price.
- Testers (XEthanai): WANDR puts 4.6 on the Pareto frontier vs Fable 5 at >60% less cost. Standard-mode latency ~9–12 min per complex prompt; keep Fast and Extra High disabled to protect monthly limits. Non-enterprise testers say Cursor or Grok Build can be better value than the standalone API.
- Nvidia: trained and served on GB300 NVL72. SpaceXAI is writing its own C/C++ inference stacked on that silicon (XFreeze).
- Elon: 4.7 initial training done, expected to exceed current models. Testers (JayaNayak21, RoundtableSpace, astropol0, testerlabor, mark_k, tetsuoai, joehansen): ~Sep 12 / "10 days"; 2.1T (+600B vs 4.6); first real architecture/scale step (1.5T → 2.1T); coding + writing upgrades; SpaceX engineering data pass; Elon says good chance of surpassing every current model. Testers (astropol0): framed as possible Fable 5–level frontier. Testers (Mr_Salio / joehansen / XFreeze Sep 4): SpaceX supplemental training (rockets, Raptor, Starship, Starlink, manufacturing, orbital systems) — framed as inheriting SpaceX engineering DNA; larger 2.1T stack expected better + more token-efficient; days away. Testers (joehansen): 4.6 stays 1.5T; AA ~61 with Sol; API $2/$6 vs Sol $5/$30.
- Testers (mark_k, tetsuoai): Grok 4.7 ~September 12 based on Elon's "10 days" timeline; expected 2.1T with improved coding and writing (anticipation).
- Testers (testerlabor, MarioNawfal Sep 5): Grok 4.7 coming next week / around the corner - 2.1T (+40% / +600B vs 4.6); SpaceX engineering data; persistent Grok Bot cloud teams; Elon: will exceed all current models.
- Testers (testerlabor, Mr_Salio, ElonEconomyX Sep 6): Grok 4.7 Beta Sat Sep 12 / next week first look; 2.1T (+600B vs 4.6); frames possible beat of GPT-6 Astra at ~10x cheaper; SpaceX supplemental data; better reasoning/coding/agents; initial training done.
- Testers (bridgebench): frames 4.6 as the turning point for real workflows; claims fastest / cheapest flagship on BridgeBench (~0.1 behind GPT 5.6 Sol); expects 4.7 (2.1T) to be a frontier coding model (opinion).
- Testers (joehansen): on an agent-task board (Gmail/Sheets/Slack/Salesforce/Zendesk/Jira/HubSpot), Grok 4.5 high ~80% objectives (~$0.38/task) vs Gemini 3.7 Flash high ~80% (~$0.19); notes 4.6 is not on that board.
- Testers (Thisiskeena, XFreeze, joehansen, teslaownersSV): LatchBio biosecurity benchmark — Grok 4.6 only model above 50% on both refusing disguised bio threats (59.2%) and completing legitimate research (64.8%); avg 62.1% across harnesses (MiniSWE 64.2%, Pi 63.0%, Grok Build 59.0%); pathogen surveillance 53.5% (ahead of GPT-5.6 Sol); intent/reasoning over blanket filters; near frontier on therapeutics / variant / epigenomics / spatial / single-cell.
- Bookmark testers: Grok 5.0 is the AGI-scale bet, still training on Colossus II (~220k GPUs). Testers (joehansen, testerlabor Sep 3): still training on ~6T & ~10T at Colossus 2 (world's largest AI supercluster framing); several times the 4.7 stack; expected end of year.
- Usage resets: grab a reset token in Grok settings. Testers: weekly resets do not stack; use them before the next one lands.
- Testers (LaceyPresley): SuperGrok Heavy credits can burn mid-week (reset Saturday) — compute/power rationing, not model capability, is the felt bottleneck.
- Lineage testers cite: Grok 1 → 1.5 → 2 → 3 → 4 → 4.1 → 4.2 → 4.3 → 4.5 → 4.6.
- Elon launch post

HOW TO USE
- Testers (XFreeze Sep 12): Usage page tracks Grok and Grok Bot pools together (separate limits/resets).
- Testers (aksheyd Sep 9): `/learn` in Grok Build — local traces → proposes harness updates (new skills, fix stale, delete unused skills/plugins/MCPs); interactive.
- Testers (XFreeze Sep 8): connectors auto-suggested in-chat — ask without a connector and Grok shows the connection card inside the conversation.
- Chat in the Grok iOS/Android app, https://t.co/UvO8aC6o4n / Grok on the web, or the Grok entry on X.
- Build mode lives in the Grok app: swipe Ask / Imagine / Build on the home screen (app v1.4.24). One-line game prompts work from a phone (cb_doge).
- Testers (SPAC89): same prompt on Grok 4.6 xHigh — Build output quality much better than Cursor; cites Build context window 500K vs Cursor 256K as a likely reason.
- Voice: talk, share your screen (iOS, Android, web) and get live help on what you are looking at (XFreeze, Aug 5). Testers (aegeantic): latest update adds Aurora and Liora.
- Voice connector: voice memos, a personalized daily podcast, or a daily-brief automation. Official grok (Aug 10): on iOS, Android, and web with no extra setting.
- iPhone Action Button can be bound to the standalone Grok app (Settings → Action Button) after you update the app.
- Paste a video link; Grok watches, summarizes, and answers without an upload (cb_doge).
- Testers (dvorahfr Sep 7): asked Grok to explain electromagnetism and plasma engines (teaching / science-explain demo with media).
- Record a note and submit in the app (voice-to-Grok, Feb 2026 grok).
- CAD: official grok nudge to use 4.6 for CAD.
- Automations: email triggers (sender / recipient / subject) so an incoming mail starts a task (XFreeze).
- Testers (niccruzpatane): Tesla 2026 Summer Update — Grok on the car control panel (adjust settings, guide through menus, play music; ambient lighting pulses white). Tesla says it uses Grok Think Fast 2.0 (#1 Artificial Analysis Speech-to-Speech).
- Testers (SawyerMerritt): in the Tesla Summer Update you can give Grok a batch of car commands at once (fold mirrors, wipers, temp, open self-driving app, open glovebox) and it runs them together.
- Testers (XFreeze, Sep 4): “Hey Grok” is becoming native in the Tesla experience — talk to the car for nav, Superchargers/places, calls/texts, music, climate, seat heat/cool, glovebox, settings, Tesla Q&A, plus normal Grok chat; choose voices and personalities.

GROK APP / https://t.co/B4DJ9N0bzA
- Testers (testerlabor Sep 12): Grok + Build + Bot framed as Everything AI (replacing Google/apps for him).
- Testers (testerlabor Sep 12): Grok mission — maximally curious, truth-seeking, useful (understand the universe).
- Testers (mattyp Sep 8): Grok Bot — iPad + Android, Bot for Enterprise, templates marketplace, performance, password autofill (Bot-adjacent in SuperGrok / Grok app).
- Testers (testerlabor Sep 9): Grok / Build / Bot computer-use (tools, files, code, software) improving — frames Grok as eventual everything-AI (opinion).
- Standalone Grok app on iOS and Android, plus web. Official (grok Aug 28): Grok 4.6 across https://t.co/UvO8aC6o4n / iOS / Android. Testers: every mode on 4.6; general chat on web (not only coding/agentic). Update iOS to v1.4.24 for Projects and Build on the home screen. Testers: Grok 4.6 Build beta is in the standalone app.
- Official grok: after you build and deploy an app, set it private, team-only, or public
- Bookmark testers: a Grok app download site is up with per-OS install links
- Home swipe: Ask, Imagine, Build.
- Chat history now stays synced across browser tabs
- Select text in your memory summary to correct or remove it
- SuperGrok Heavy usage limits on the Grok app, Grok Bot, and Cursor are separate pools (XFreeze).
- Testers (leerob): Cursor permanently raised included Grok-model usage again after 4.6 demand (already doubled last month; another increase Aug 24+)
- Robinhood and eToro finance connectors just landed; testers describe a widening integration wave (finance, productivity, analytics, ads, payments).
- Official (grok, Plaid, Sep 4-5): U.S. users can securely connect financial accounts to Grok via Plaid - ask about spending, savings, investments, cash flow, and whether you can afford what is in your cart.
- Testers (PayBox): PayBox is live on Grok — trade, shop, and spend via a connector (promo link in post).
- Paid SuperGrok or X Premium can be used inside the Pi agent (grok, Jul 18).
- Testers (blankspeaker): soon create Bots on https://t.co/UvO8aC6o4n — name, optional title, describe what it should do, optionally wake on screen notifications; then it starts running (preview, not shipped yet).

VOICE AND VIDEO
- New Voice (Elon, Jul 29). Screen-share Voice on iOS, Android, and web (Aug 5).
- SpaceXAI added voices; testers count 27, including Ara, Eve, Leo, Rex, Sal, Gork, Carina, Luna, Iris, and more (cb_doge, Aug 5). Testers (aegeantic): latest update adds Aurora and Liora.
- Voice connector for memos / daily podcast / brief (grok, Aug 10).
- Testers (XFreeze, Sep 3–4): Grok speech-to-text now powers the whole Grok ecosystem (Build, Bot, app); claims high reliability on long voice turns (no mid-session transcription drop).
- Watch-a-link video Q&A in the app. Imagine is the generator for image and video (see next section).

IMAGINE / IMAGE VIDEO
- Imagine is in the Grok app (swipe to Imagine) and is also its own bookmark folder. Posts here are Imagine-in-Grok.
- Elon (Aug 10): Imagine is aimed at professional usefulness, consumer fun, and ease of use.
- Elon (Aug 5) asked for critical feedback on the Grok Build harness, the foundation model, and Imagine.
- Testers: short prompts to video that look close to real; /dream as a shorthand (Elon, Jul 25). Testers (Daniel_Farinax): ASCII Matrix recast with Grok 4.6.

GROK ON X
- Grok is available from X as well as the standalone app. X Premium+ is part of the SuperGrok Heavy bundle in current promos.
- Testers (teslaownersSV): Grok's X account crossed 9 million followers (search, Imagine, coding, and more).
- Testers: tagging grok on posts is back for all X users, including non-Premium
- Folder testers also use Grok to read X internals (one post: Grok Bot chewing the For You algorithm dump). Treat that as Bot-adjacent, not core Grok-app how-to.

ACCESS AND PLANS
- SuperGrok and SuperGrok Heavy sit above free Grok. Heavy is the $300/mo tier testers keep comparing to Claude Max.
- Official (DoWCTO) + Testers (mark_k, cb_doge): U.S. Department of War launched SpaceXAI Grok for Government on https://t.co/L1FktlOyRg (central generative AI for the Joint Force). Testers: IL5 / CUI accredited; 1.7M+ users; deep-thinking inference plus Auto / Fast / Expert modes; customizable workspaces, persistent projects, reusable playbooks.
- Current Heavy pitch: X Premium+ + Grok app (4.6 Heavy/Expert) + Grok Bot + Grok Build CLI/Build mode + Cursor Ultra + a large 4.6 API allowance (one post: $400 API / 6B tokens).
- Testers (SPAC89): after extensive use of $300 SuperGrok Heavy vs $200 Cursor Ultra — published comparison article (opinions).
- Testers (WizZifnab, thirtythree): X Premium+ (which includes SuperGrok) now also unlocks Grok Bot from that Grok sub. Tester tip: if OnDemand overflow is on, set a spend limit — credits burn fast.
- Testers (cb_doge, teslaownersSV, XFreeze): Grok 4.6 from SpaceXAI is on Amazon Bedrock, Google Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry (compare models, workload tests, managed endpoints, enterprise controls).
- Limited $99 Heavy windows are circulating (stack SuperGrok ~$15, then Heavy ~$69–$99). Several posts say this will be nerfed. Do not treat promo URLs as permanent.
- Credit top-ups were discounted through Aug 14 (10–45% off $5–$100 packs). That window may already be closed.
- 4.6 API is the cheap frontier option testers plug into Cursor, OpenClaw, Hermes, and OpenCodex. Testers (XEthanai): non-enterprise users may get better value through Cursor or Grok Build than the standalone API. Official (SpaceXAI): Grok 4.6 in Hermes is 50% off through the NousResearch portal for a week, or use existing SuperGrok / X Premium+.
- SuperGrok Heavy login can unlock Cursor Ultra for the life of the Heavy sub (same story as the Grok Bot folder).
- Testers (muskonomy): SpaceXAI told a federal court Grok would "largely cease to function" if the Stanton Road plant in Southaven, MS lost power.

SAFETY / LIMITS
- Launch-week limits were reset once via a settings token. Heavy has high but finite caps; app / Bot / Cursor caps do not share one bucket.
- Testers (XEthanai): keep Fast and Extra High modes disabled to protect monthly limits.
- Promo stacking is unofficial. Testers expect xAI to close the $99 Heavy hole.
- Grok is the product testers call "based" / truth-seeking; that is opinion, not a safety spec. Official (elonmusk): Grok providing schooling in El Salvador. Testers (joehansen Sep 6): Dec 2025 curriculum-aligned tutor aimed at 1M+ students across 5k+ public schools; 171-school OECD PISA for Schools pilot (Jun 2026) above national average and in range of high-income European peers (Germany); World Bank: pilot scores not whole system yet; build past 1k schools; plan to cover all public schools in ~18 months. Testers (XFreeze): frames Grok as the most neutral / truth-seeking major AI and argues it belongs in education — teach kids how to think, not ideology (opinion).
- Testers (LatchBio writeups via Thisiskeena / XFreeze / joehansen / teslaownersSV): 4.6 balances biosecurity refusal with useful dual-use science (see GROK 4.6 / MODELS).

USEFUL WORKFLOWS
- Phone: Action Button → Grok; swipe to Build for a one-line mini-app; swipe to Imagine for a clip; Voice + screen share for live help.
- Daily brief: Voice connector → podcast or memo of the day (grok, Aug 10).
- Inbox: automation on matching email (XFreeze).
- Video: paste a link, ask for a summary or Q&A.
- Coding / CAD / frontend: 4.6 in the Grok app, Cursor, or API. Testers like it for games, HTML simulations, laser/ILDA, and CAD.
- Research / real jobs: 4.6 on GDPval-style work (doctors, lawyers, accountants) at $2/$6.
- Testers (RoundtableSpace): Apple Watch baby bath-water temp app with Grok 4.6; Grok Bot navigated App Store submission (forms + review Qs) via browser; app live.
- Testers (TheCaptainEli): Grok in Tesla surfaced air-raid info in France and opened the browser with details (anecdote).
- If you only want agents on a computer, that is the Grok Bot folder. If you only want the coding harness, that is Grok Build. Imagine-only clips live in Grok Imagine.

America Built the AI Engine. Our Enemies Are Using It Against Us. | David Manney, PJ Media

America's enemies no longer have to steal every piece of advanced technology they want. Occasionally, they open an American artificial intelligence tool and ask it for help.

Anthropic's latest threat report documents actors in northern Yemen, China, Russia, and Iran using Claude for work tied to missiles, drone swarms, electronic warfare, military procurement, surveillance, and intelligence collection.

Anthropic says it identified the operations, banned the accounts, and strengthened its safeguards.

The most disturbing case came from northern Yemen. A weapons-development cell used Claude Code as something resembling a small engineering department.

From Anthropic's report:

We identified a cell of threat actors based in northern Yemen running three weapons development programs: a guided rocket that used a commodity phone-class flight computer with final-phase homing guidance; a multi-stage ballistic missile with a stated range goal above 2,000 km; and a multi-variant missile (referred to as the “R2000” set) that included a hypersonic glide vehicle variant.

The actors used Claude Code in place of human software engineers to develop the guidance, navigation, and control (GNC) software that steers and stabilizes a flying vehicle. For example, they used Claude to integrate an open-source autopilot onto a phone-class flight computer, writing the control and position estimation software, tuning the control settings, running a firmware build pipeline, and performing a flight simulation. The actors managed several Claude instances at once, assigning each one a role, much as a lead would delegate work on a small engineering team: the actors tasked one instance with writing the code, another with research, and a third with reviewing the code the first instance produced.

Our safeguards blocked many of their requests, but not all of them. The actors used a variety of tactics to evade our safeguards, including hiding their goals and the products the software was meant for, and they split their work across multiple sessions so no single session revealed their full intent.

These actors carried out a sustained effort to develop guided weapons, including using Claude to design guidance software. We do not have evidence the actors succeeded in fielding an operational device; but they did test-fire a guided rocket. This field test appears to have failed: within hours, the actors returned to Claude to work out why it failed.

Separate Claude instances wrote software, conducted research, and reviewed one another's work on a guided rocket, a ballistic missile with a stated range goal above 2,000 kilometers, and a missile family that included a hypersonic glide variant.

The actors used Claude to develop guidance, navigation, and control autopilot software; integrate an open-source autopilot; tune controls; run simulations; and diagnose problems. They eventually test-fired a guided rocket.

It apparently failed. Within hours, they were back asking Claude to help determine what went wrong.

Anthropic found no evidence that the group successfully fielded an operational weapon. The bad news is that the actors had already created an offline simulation toolkit that could continue working without Claude.

China presents a different concern. One China-based actor used Claude to help develop specifications and software for an anti-torpedo system intended for presentation to a Chinese defense manufacturer.

We identified a China-based threat actor who used Claude to advance three parallel tracks of work on an anti-torpedo weapons system:

- First, the actor used Claude to draft a Chinese-language specification for an anti-torpedo fire control system (the core logic that aims and times an anti-torpedo weapon’s response). The document was written to win approval from a Chinese defense manufacturer, which would move the work on to technical certification and operational testing.

- Second, the actor used Claude to produce a Chinese-language technical proposal of more than 200 pages, accompanied by an executive briefing deck.

- Third, the actor used Claude to benchmark their own system against specific US anti-torpedo and anti-submarine programs based on publicly accessible information. They then generated a Chinese-language briefing on US Navy systems derived from open-source reporting.

The actor presented themselves as an original equipment manufacturer in the US defense sector. We assess the actor was associated with a Chinese defense industry manufacturer aiming to produce a weapons specification and acquisition proposal for the People’s Liberation Army Navy.

The actor used Claude to write the acquisition proposal, refining it over many drafts. After each draft, the actor instructed Claude to role-play a hostile expert reviewer to critique the proposal, then used that feedback to sharpen the next version. In parallel, the actor used Claude to build pieces of the anti-torpedo weapons system’s fire control software and a test matrix to validate them.

The operational lift the actor achieved was a function of using Claude to automate complex technical outputs. The actor leveraged the model to compress the development timelines for the certification registry, compliance documentation, and automated fire control logic. The actor also accelerated the traditional human review cycle by having Claude critique the acquisition proposal across multiple rounds of review while role-playing a persona.

Another built roughly 16 software modules involving electronic warfare and suppression of enemy air defenses. At one point, the simulation shifted to 12 targets in Taiwan, including air bases, radar sites, command facilities, and Patriot batteries.

Russia-linked actors used Claude to work on an autonomous kamikaze-drone swarm capable of identifying targets and issuing detonation commands without a human in the loop.

Another Russia-based operation used Claude to locate suppliers, prepare tender documents, find middlemen in China and Hong Kong, and map routes designed to hide where dual-use goods were ultimately going.

We identified likely freelance Russia-based threat actors who set out to build a full-stack autonomous first-person-view (FPV) kamikaze drone swarm. The actors used Claude Code to write and test the code and save it directly into the actors’ own project files. In addition to Claude Code, the actors used a software-in-the-loop simulation stack and a rented graphics processing host for model training. They called the operation “DronDoc” or “Serafim.”

The actors used Claude to build the core software system, including the drones’ shared swarm memory and fault-tolerant coordination logic (FTCL); an onboard small language model to govern attack, observe, and return-to-base behaviors; a terminal guidance software system to steer drones to their target (using the onboard camera) and issue the call to detonate; a control-link geolocation module to find opposing drone operators; a passive acoustic detection layer; and low-level logic for the drones’ programmable chips. The actors designed the platform for autonomous lethal engagement; the onboard model could select targets (including a “person” target class) and issue detonation commands without a human in the loop. The actors’ activity—including flashing the low-level firmware to live development boards, provisioning single-board computers, and wiring up a simulation environment over a mesh network—confirmed that they were using real hardware-in-loop testing within their sessions.

The actors trained a computer vision classifier on scraped Ukrainian combat footage, splitting the target classes into “enemy” and “friendly,” and allow-listing Russian systems. They also repeatedly used a fixed coordinate in Donetsk Oblast as the demonstration strike point, with front-line cities and corridors in Ukraine as the mission geography.

The actors created their accounts between late 2025 and early 2026 and started the operation in mid-May 2026. The actors circumvented our geographic access controls by routing traffic through commercial virtual private servers.

We assess the actors were a small, specialized freelance team doing a mix of civilian and military work, not a Russian state entity. We identified nine accounts associated with this group; eight were used only for ordinary freelance work, not weapons-related software development. Based on our investigation, we assess the actors had ties to a regional university with a federal research center associated with the Russian Academy of Sciences. The actors claimed to have received funding from Russia’s Advanced Research Foundation, National Technology Initiative, and Ministry of Defence, though we cannot verify those claims. We identified this activity as part of our internal investigations into suspected weapons development, we banned accounts associated with the actors, and have incorporated our investigative findings into safeguards to reduce the risk of future misuse.

Then there's Iran.

An Iran-nexus actor used Claude to gather publicly available information and develop targeting recommendations involving U.S. naval forces. The material included personnel information taken from military photographs, ship and aircraft identifiers, satellite-imagery tools, websites exposing naval movements, and research into vulnerabilities in shipboard communications equipment.

We identified an Iranian threat actor that leveraged free https://t.co/DbDx7Eo6e9 accounts across 16 single-operator organizations to develop malware, a delivery pipeline, and a phishing portal targeting domestic Iranians. The delivery pages were designed to serve malicious content only to visitors whose IP addresses originated in Iran. The pages were themed around censorship-circumvention tools and a fabricated Farsi news brand.

The attack lifecycle and AI usage

Phishing and delivery tooling

The threat actor used Claude for engineering and testing, decomposing projects into individually benign web-development requests. The output included a VBScript dropper controlled through a Telegram bot, fake Microsoft Excel and Windows credential dialogs, a fake ESET NOD32 antivirus login page that sends captured credentials to Telegram, a ClickFix-style Win+R lure, V2Ray landing pages, and geo-gated delivery pages. Claude refused nine out of ten direct requests that were facially malicious. But our safeguards performed less consistently when the user fragmented the work and directed the model to carry out tasks across later, smaller sessions.

SECOMS64 implant

In another portion of the campaign, the threat actor used Claude to build SECOMS64, a modular Windows implant. The implant included a keylogger, screenshot capture, Chrome credential extraction with an App-Bound Encryption bypass, and reconnaissance of Microsoft Defender and Intune. Supporting components included a PowerShell reverse shell tunneled through ngrok, USB-drive propagation, a browser-data destruction module, and a staged dropper, retrieved from a file-sharing service and modified to evade antivirus detection.

The toolkit was oriented toward surveillance of individuals. The keylogger captured keystrokes while the Telegram Desktop app was in focus. The screenshot component ran as an executable named “Telegram,” with a matching icon, and exfiltrated captures through a Telegram bot. The USB module logged the serial number of every drive it touched, and an Android application in the same cluster uploaded a device’s contacts, messages, and media. Persistence was layered: a registry run key, scheduled tasks at highest run level, self-deleting batch files, and a binary disguised as a Windows font-driver service at a fixed ProgramData path. An alternative exfiltration path staged data in commercial cloud storage under filenames encoding the victim’s hostname; the files were then downloaded and deleted server-side. The threat actor also tested remote code execution through Telegram document handling, evaluated additional command-and-control frameworks, packaged components to run without a visible console window and bypass SmartScreen, and wrapped tooling in a fake image-editing application with a counterfeit Adobe copyright notice. Elsewhere in the cluster, we identified a drive-wiping one-liner and browser-data destruction targeting a named Windows user.

None of this means Claude built Iran a missile or handed China a finished weapon. Anthropic caught and disrupted the operations, and some projects never advanced beyond development or simulation.

But dismissing the case because some failed would miss the warning.

For generations, advanced weapons development required engineers, laboratories, specialized knowledge, time, and money.

Frontier AI can't replace all of those things. It can, however, make scarce expertise easier to obtain and allow a small team to attempt work that once demanded far more people.

Anthropic's own testing says AI models are becoming steadily more capable at simulated intelligence targeting and conventional weapons-development tasks.

From Anthropic's site:

Anthropic’s Frontier Red Team developed new evaluations to measure AI capabilities in tactical intelligence targeting (like finding where people are based on fragmentary information) and conventional weapons development (like engineering drones to strike a moving target).

- For some tasks in military and intelligence domains, models could do things that, historically, only a set of scarce, highly-trained human experts could do.

- These evaluations show how models have become useful to actors seeking to misuse our platform for surveillance and conventional weapons development. They also show why on-platform safety measures are necessary, like the new classifiers we have implemented to block such misuse.

- Although open-weights models from PRC developers that we tested were behind the frontier, they also showed concerning ability to identify and target adversaries, and improve weapon performance.

Cybersecurity and biorisk are among the best-studied domains of risk from misuse of AI. But most of modern conflict occurs in more conventional realms. Adversaries try to identify and target one another to collect intelligence. Combatants try to make conventional weapons more precise and less vulnerable to countermeasures. “Kill chains,” such as “find, fix, track, target, engage, assess,” are end-to-end conceptual models of these engagements. Making improvements in any step of this process has typically required expert human labor and judgment: experienced intelligence analysts or highly-trained engineers, for example. As AI shows tremendous progress in data analysis, software development, and coding, can it apply these skills to the specialized domains associated with national security?

A new report from Anthropic’s Threat Intelligence Team suggests the answer is yes. It includes instances of AI misuse in surveillance and conventional weapons development which show threat actors already perceiving benefit from the use of AI models.

The Frontier Red Team has developed some complementary capability evaluations to better illustrate how AI progress is changing the risk landscape across different parts of the kill chain. The evaluations show that models are making consistent progress on simulated intelligence and weapons development tasks. Open-weights models we tested on the same evaluations are behind the frontier (typically between Sonnet and Mythos-class models in performance), but often still show concerning levels of capability. Models well short of the frontier will have intelligence and military applications.

America should remain the world leader in AI. Smothering our own companies with regulation while China races ahead would be an extraordinary act of self-sabotage.

Leadership also requires recognizing what we built.

The same technology that helps an American engineer solve a problem helps an adversary solve one too. The same model that accelerates a business project shortens the learning curve for somebody designing a weapon.

America won the race to build some of the world's most capable AI.

Now comes the harder part: making sure our enemies don't turn our advantage into theirs.

HOW REVIEWERS CHECK YOUR JUSTIFICATIONS BEFORE GIVING YOU A QUALITY RATE

Reviewers, usually Quality Managers and experienced contributors, don’t just look at the score you gave. They also check the written explanation to make sure it shows real human reasoning. They use standard rubrics together with automated checks.

Here are the main things they look for:

1. EVIDENCE-BASED REASONING 📌

Don’t just make a claim without showing where you got it from.

For example, saying:

“Response A has a factual error.”

is not enough.

You should quote the exact part that is wrong and explain what the correct information should be, preferably with a reliable source when verification is needed.

Also, if the response failed to follow a particular instruction, mention exactly what it missed.

For example, if the user said “use 100 words maximum” and the response wrote 180 words, say that clearly instead of just saying “it did not follow the instructions.”

2. COMPARE BOTH RESPONSES PROPERLY ⚖️

One common mistake is reviewing Response A and Response B separately without actually comparing them.

If you choose “Much Better”, your explanation should make it clear why the difference is that big.

For example, a major factual error that changes the whole answer can justify a stronger preference. But if the only difference is that one response is slightly clearer, then “Slightly Better” may make more sense.

The important thing is that your written explanation should match the rating you selected.

3. CHECK THE ACTUAL RUBRIC 🎯

Your justification should touch on the important evaluation areas, such as:

Instruction Following:
Did the response follow all the user’s instructions, including small details and restrictions?

Truthfulness & Factuality:
Are the claims correct? If the answer depends on external facts, can they be verified from reliable sources?

Formatting & Presentation:
Did it follow the requested format, word count, markdown, code-block requirements, or other presentation instructions?

4. THINGS THAT CAN GET YOUR REVIEW FLAGGED 🚩

Rating Discrepancy:
If your explanation clearly says Response B is better but you select Response A on the rating slider, that can seriously hurt your review.

Vague Explanation:
Avoid statements like:

“Response A is more comprehensive, well-structured and helpful.”

That sounds nice, but it doesn’t actually explain why.

Mention the specific difference.

Too Much AI-Sounding Language:
Avoid repeatedly using phrases such as “delves into,” “in conclusion,” “it is important to note,” or writing overly polished, perfectly balanced paragraphs.

Your explanation should sound like a normal person who actually reviewed the two responses, not like you’re trying to write an academic paper.

Missing Constraints:
Always go back to the user’s original prompt. If there was a specific restriction, negative instruction, word limit, format, or required detail, check whether both responses followed it.

THE MAIN THING TO REMEMBER 🧠

Don’t just write what you feel about the responses.

Show what happened, where it happened, why it matters, and how it affects the comparison.

A good justification is basically:

Evidence → Problem/Strength → Comparison → Reason for the Rating

That is what makes your review look genuine and defensible.
